Meeting header: 2026-08-12 15:00 PDT | Duration: 52 mins | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Jordan (Veridian Head of ML), Priya (Veridian SRE), Samir (CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro - I'm Maya on AE, Carlos is our solutions engineer. Jordan, do you want to do a quick intro on your side?
[00:10] Jordan: Yeah hi, Jordan here. we run ML infra at Veridian Payments, several fraud and risk models, and starting to put large language models into customer support and document analysis. timeline Q4 pilot then production in Q1.
[00:22] Priya: Priya here, SRE, i'll be focused on networking/VPC and isolation requirements.
[00:27] Samir: Samir, CTO, interested in cost and operational overhead.
[00:32] Carlos: Awesome. goal for today is to understand your requirements for Dedicated capacity - reserved GPUs, isolation, burst strategy, scaling - and see fit vs hosted or private.

Summary
[00:45] Maya: quick recap of what we heard in the signup: you currently run some on-prem GPUs for real-time scoring, you evaluated in-house alternatives and Replicate, and you want a reserved capacity plan for predictable throughput and data isolation. correct?
[00:58] Jordan: Yep, basically. We want isolation from other tenants, predictable latency for customer-facing flows, and ability to burst for batch/ingest processing.

Topics
- current infra and traffic patterns
- strictness of data isolation and compliance needs
- burst/queue strategy and autoscaling expectations
- cost / unit economics and tradeoffs
- next steps: pricing, benchmarks, networking deep-dive

Transcript body
[01:25] Carlos: Let's start with traffic - can you describe request profile: qps, model sizes, token lengths?
[01:31] Jordan: For the customer support generation route we expect 6 to 12 qps steady during business hours, with spikes up to ~50 qps for outage incidents. average prompt length 80 to 200 tokens, responses 50 to 150 tokens. we also plan nightly ingest jobs that will do large batch embedding/reranking - those will be more throughput-oriented, maybe 2000 requests over an hour.
[01:56] Priya: Important: all inference needs to stay in our VPC, logs must be forwarded to our SIEM, and all keys stored in our KMS. SOC 2 is table stakes.
[02:07] Maya: Totally - Redwood Dedicated supports VPC peering/private networking and KMS integrations; we can do logs to your SIEM and provide audit logs. we'll include SOC2 and architecture docs in the follow-up.
[02:20] Jordan: Side question - what's the dif between Dedicated and Private? we read docs but want clarifications on isolation and upgrade surface.
[02:28] Carlos: Good question. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools in our managed infra - physical isolation by allocation and tenant tagging but runs in Redwood-managed hosts; Private is customer-deployed control plane (VPC or on-prem) where you own the infra and we provide the software+ops layer. Dedicated is faster to start and lower ops for you; Private gives max isolation and control but higher integration effort.
[02:56] Samir: For us, data residency and audit controls might push us to Private later, but for pilot we prefer Dedicated to reduce integration work.
[03:05] Maya: sounds common. let's talk SLA and latency SLOs - what are your p95 targets?
[03:11] Jordan: p95 < 150ms for generation calls is ideal; p99 we can accept up to ~300ms. for batch embeddings latency not critical but throughput matters.
[03:21] Carlos: p95 150ms is aggressive but achievable with pinned models and warm KV cache. we'll recommend model variants and quantization to hit throughput. Key levers: batching size, continuous KV caching, and pre-warmed workers.
[03:36] Priya: On warm workers - how does Redwood handle cold starts and burst capacity? we need to absorb sudden spikes without huge tail latency.
[03:44] Carlos: Dedicated offers configurable burst capacity and automatic warm pools. you get a base reserved pool sized for steady qps and a burst pool that can spin up - there's a tradeoff: more reserved capacity lowers tail latency and cost predictability; burst reduces cost but can increase transient latency during spin-up. we also support instant fallback to compatible model variants in other regions if capacity exhausted.
[04:07] Jordan: what's the typical spin-up time for a new worker/GPU?
[04:11] Carlos: usually under 90 seconds for warm pool scale-up with cached weights; full cold boot can be a few minutes. but we recommend pre-warming the KV cache for critical routes. for incident spikes, the burst pool should handle most cases.
[04:25] Maya: also note we provide automatic scaling policies and can set a 'burst budget' per month to cap spend.

Objections / tradeoffs
[04:36] Samir: our CFO cares about cost predictability - how do we model unit costs vs self-hosting?
[04:42] Maya: we'll send a detailed spreadsheet showing per-token/unit economics across dedicated sizes and burst behavior. key variables: effective batch factor, token throughput per GPU for your model, and cache hit rates. for many customers, Dedicated reduces TCO vs self-hosting when accounting for ops and utilization.
[05:01] Jordan: Another concern: model updates - we need canary rollouts and ability to pin versions for regulated flows.
[05:08] Carlos: Redwood has rollout controls: canary %, A/B, instant rollback, and model pinning per route. we also support immutable model bundles and audit trail for which model served each request.
[05:19] Priya: security deep-dive: do you support customer-managed keys (CMK) for encryption at rest?
[05:24] Maya: yes, CMK via KMS integrations; we can provide HSM-backed KMS where required and provide audit logs for key usage.

Technical details and examples
[05:35] Carlos: for sizing example - given your target p95 150ms and steady 10 qps, with avg sequence 150 tokens and our perf profile of model X-8B (~120 tokens/sec per GPU after quantization), we'd recommend a base pool of 2-3 GPUs with a 2-GPU burst buffer to hit spikes. for embeddings batch jobs we'll schedule separate worker queues to avoid impacting low-latency routes.
[06:05] Jordan: can you share the perf profile and quantization guidance?
[06:09] Carlos: we'll attach the model perf sheet in follow-up; generally quantized 4-bit variants yield 2-3x throughput improvements with small accuracy tradeoffs - we'll propose candidate variants and can run evals on your prompt set.

Network and compliance
[06:22] Priya: network egress and ingress - we need all traffic restricted to our VPC and support for private endpoints, no public internet for inference nodes.
[06:30] Maya: Dedicated supports private networking, private endpoints, and VPC peering; we can lock inference plane inside customer VPC with a private control plane connection. we'll run a network checklist and provide required firewall rules.

Procurement and timeline
[06:46] Samir: procurement question - minimum commitment for Dedicated?
[06:50] Maya: typical entry is monthly reserved commitments for GPUs (1-3 month minimum depending on region) and we can structure a 3-6 month pilot with credits and capped burst budget. we'll include contract templates and a rough pricing example.

Recap and explicit next steps
[07:05] Maya: recap - Veridian wants Dedicated for pilot: isolation, predictable latency, burst for incident peaks, VPC/KMS/SOC2 compliance. next we will: 1) send pricing & sizing spreadsheet, 2) share SOC2 and architecture docs, 3) schedule network deep-dive with Priya and Carlos next week, 4) plan a 2-week benchmark (Redwood runs baseline with sample traces). action owners: Maya, Carlos, Jordan.
[07:35] Jordan: sounds good. can you also include a simple cost comparison vs our current self-hosted numbers?
[07:40] Maya: yes will include that in the pricing sheet.

[07:47] Priya: one last thing - we need audit / retention options for logs and the ability to redact PII at rest.
[07:53] Carlos: we have data retention controls and can add PII redaction at the ingestion layer - we'll add this to the security docs.

Closing
[08:03] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll send the follow-ups by Friday (2026-08-14). schedule network deep-dive invites now.
[08:10] Samir: thanks, appreciate it.
[08:12] Jordan: thanks all.
